claims.statement: Ubaid villages and towns: approximately 5500–4000 BCE.

value.text: Ubaid villages and towns: approximately 5500–4000 BCE.

claims.statement: Ubaid communities used irrigation and fishing; some villages grew into towns centred on monumental buildings, including Eridu and Uruk.

value.text: Ubaid communities used irrigation and fishing; some villages grew into towns centred on monumental buildings, including Eridu and Uruk.

claims.statement: Mesopotamia’s Uruk period: approximately 4000–3100 BCE.

value.text: Mesopotamia’s Uruk period: approximately 4000–3100 BCE.

claims.statement: Cities developed around monumental mud-brick temples; administrative practices changed with writing on clay and the use of cylinder seals.

value.text: Cities developed around monumental mud-brick temples; administrative practices changed with writing on clay and the use of cylinder seals.

claims.statement: Building Avebury: approximately 2850–2200 BCE.

value.text: Building Avebury: approximately 2850–2200 BCE.

claims.statement: Avebury includes banks, ditches and stone circles; the precise sequence of construction remains incompletely understood.

value.text: Avebury includes banks, ditches and stone circles; the precise sequence of construction remains incompletely understood.

claims.statement: Village life at Skara Brae: approximately 3100–2500 BCE.

value.text: Village life at Skara Brae: approximately 3100–2500 BCE.

claims.statement: Skara Brae’s stone houses preserve hearths, beds and storage furniture. The inhabitants farmed, hunted and fished and made tools, pottery and jewellery.

value.text: Skara Brae’s stone houses preserve hearths, beds and storage furniture. The inhabitants farmed, hunted and fished and made tools, pottery and jewellery.

claims.statement: Building Newgrange and the Boyne tombs: approximately 3200 BCE.

value.text: Building Newgrange and the Boyne tombs: approximately 3200 BCE.

claims.statement: Newgrange, Knowth and Dowth are prehistoric passage tombs in Brú na Bóinne, whose carved stones preserve megalithic art.

value.text: Newgrange, Knowth and Dowth are prehistoric passage tombs in Brú na Bóinne, whose carved stones preserve megalithic art.

claims.statement: Yangshao communities: approximately 5000–3000 BCE.

value.text: Yangshao communities: approximately 5000–3000 BCE.

claims.statement: The National Museum of China lists Yangshao painted pottery, stone knives and mortar, spindle whorls and bone needles.

value.text: The National Museum of China lists Yangshao painted pottery, stone knives and mortar, spindle whorls and bone needles.

claims.statement: Liangzhu’s city and waterworks: approximately 3300–2300 BCE.

value.text: Liangzhu’s city and waterworks: approximately 3300–2300 BCE.

claims.statement: Liangzhu combined rice cultivation, urban planning, earthen monuments and water management. Differences in burials express social hierarchy.

value.text: Liangzhu combined rice cultivation, urban planning, earthen monuments and water management. Differences in burials express social hierarchy.

claims.statement: Malta’s megalithic temples: approximately 4000–2001 BCE.

value.text: Malta’s megalithic temples: approximately 4000–2001 BCE.

claims.statement: Malta and Gozo’s temple complexes combine upright slabs and horizontal stonework, often approached through forecourts; plans and decoration vary.

value.text: Malta and Gozo’s temple complexes combine upright slabs and horizontal stonework, often approached through forecourts; plans and decoration vary.

claims.statement: Communities before the kingdom of Kerma: approximately 3500–2500 BCE.

value.text: Communities before the kingdom of Kerma: approximately 3500–2500 BCE.

claims.statement: Pre-Kerma settlement included a large enclosure, interpreted as protection for people and wealth. Evidence for wider Upper Nubian connections remains limited.

value.text: Pre-Kerma settlement included a large enclosure, interpreted as protection for people and wealth. Evidence for wider Upper Nubian connections remains limited.

claims.statement: The kingdom of Kerma: approximately 2500–1500 BCE.

value.text: The kingdom of Kerma: approximately 2500–1500 BCE.

claims.statement: Kerma was the centre of a Nubian kingdom south of Egypt, near the Nile’s Third Cataract. Its capital and eastern cemetery preserve evidence spanning roughly 2500–1500 BCE.

value.text: Kerma was the centre of a Nubian kingdom south of Egypt, near the Nile’s Third Cataract. Its capital and eastern cemetery preserve evidence spanning roughly 2500–1500 BCE.

claims.statement: Early cultivation at Kuk: approximately 5000–4490 BCE.

value.text: Early cultivation at Kuk: approximately 5000–4490 BCE.

claims.statement: At Kuk in the New Guinea highlands, people cultivated plants on raised mounds along wetland margins. Research dates this phase to about 5000–4490 BCE and identifies intensive banana cultivation.

value.text: At Kuk in the New Guinea highlands, people cultivated plants on raised mounds along wetland margins. Research dates this phase to about 5000–4490 BCE and identifies intensive banana cultivation.

claims.statement: Ditched cultivation at Kuk: approximately 2400–2030 BCE.

value.text: Ditched cultivation at Kuk: approximately 2400–2030 BCE.

claims.statement: Later farmers at Kuk used ditches to cultivate wet ground. The research dates the beginning of this phase to about 2400–2030 BCE.

value.text: Later farmers at Kuk used ditches to cultivate wet ground. The research dates the beginning of this phase to about 2400–2030 BCE.

claims.statement: Watson Brake’s mound builders: approximately 3500–2800 BCE.

value.text: Watson Brake’s mound builders: approximately 3500–2800 BCE.

claims.statement: Watson Brake has eleven mounds and connecting ridges. Building was episodic. Food remains include nuts, fish and deer and indicate broad-spectrum foraging.

value.text: Watson Brake has eleven mounds and connecting ridges. Building was episodic. Food remains include nuts, fish and deer and indicate broad-spectrum foraging.
